claim: Porokeratosis (PK) is a heterogeneous group of keratinization disorders.
source: Porokeratosis (PK, MIM 175800) is a heterogeneous group of keratinization disorders that exhibit an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about PK presented in the introduction, drawing from established medical knowledge.

claim: PK exhibits an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance.
source: Porokeratosis (PK, MIM 175800) is a heterogeneous group of keratinization disorders that exhibit an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance.
evidence: This is a statement about the inheritance pattern of PK, drawing from established medical knowledge.

claim: PK is a skin-specific autoinflammatory disease which was often inherited and linked to ultraviolet light exposure and immunosuppression.
source: PK is also a skin-specific autoinflammatory disease which was often inherited and linked to ultraviolet light exposure and immunosuppression (Schamroth et al., 1997; Abramovits and Oquendo, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Schamroth et al., 1997; Abramovits and Oquendo, 2013).

claim: Eruptive pruritic papular porokeratosis exemplifies the inflammatory manifestation of PK.
source: For example, eruptive pruritic papular porokeratosis exemplifies the inflammatory manifestation, and complications to inflammatory conditions such as localized cutaneous amyloidosis are seen in PK patients (Biswas, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Biswas, 2015.

claim: Complications to inflammatory conditions such as localized cutaneous amyloidosis are seen in PK patients.
source: For example, eruptive pruritic papular porokeratosis exemplifies the inflammatory manifestation, and complications to inflammatory conditions such as localized cutaneous amyloidosis are seen in PK patients (Biswas, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Biswas, 2015.

claim: PK and psoriasis share some features at both clinical and molecular levels.
source: Indeed, PK and psoriasis share some features at both clinical and molecular levels and sometimes coexist in the same patients (Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2008.

claim: PK and psoriasis sometimes coexist in the same patients.
source: Indeed, PK and psoriasis share some features at both clinical and molecular levels and sometimes coexist in the same patients (Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2008.

claim: Cornoid lamella (CL) is a vertical 'column' of parakeratosis that serves as a histological hallmark unifying all variants of PK.
source: As a histological hallmark that unifies all variants of PK, cornoid lamella (CL) is a vertical 'column' of parakeratosis.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the histological feature of PK, drawing from established medical knowledge.

claim: The pattern of CL can be slender, broad, or confluent, which is related to epidermal hyperplasia and dermal inflammation.
source: The pattern of CL can be slender, broad, or confluent, which is related to epidermal hyperplasia and dermal inflammation.
evidence: This claim describes the relationship between CL patterns and tissue changes, drawing from established medical knowledge.

claim: CL is not a unique feature of PK because it can be seen in some inflammatory and inherited cutaneous disorders and also as an incidental finding.
source: However, CL is not a unique feature of PK because it can be seen in some inflammatory and inherited cutaneous disorders and also as an incidental finding (Biswas, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Biswas, 2015.

claim: PK is currently classified according to the clinical manifestations, such as number, size, morphology, and distribution of the histological lesions.
source: PK is currently classified according to the clinical manifestations, such as number, size, morphology, and distribution of the histological lesions.
evidence: This describes the current classification system for PK, drawing from established medical knowledge.

claim: Some variants of PK are fraught with confusing terminology.
source: A better system of classification is expected because some variants of PK are fraught with confusing terminology (Schamroth et al., 1997; Sertznig et al., 2012; Biswas, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Schamroth et al., 1997; Sertznig et al., 2012; Biswas, 2015).

claim: It is sometimes hard to completely differentiate disseminated superficial actinic porokeratosis (DSAP) from disseminated superficial porokeratosis (DSP) by age of onset and sun-exposed areas.
source: For example, it is sometimes hard to completely differentiate disseminated superficial actinic porokeratosis (DSAP) from disseminated superficial porokeratosis (DSP) by age of onset and sun-exposed areas.
evidence: This is an observation about the difficulty in differentiating PK variants, drawing from clinical knowledge.

claim: At least five linkage loci (i.e., 12q23.2-24.1, 15q25.1-26.1, 18p11.3, 1p31.3-p31.1, 16q24.1-24.3) have been reported for the disseminated forms of PK.
source: At least five linkage loci (i.e., 12q23.2-24.1, 15q25.1-26.1, 18p11.3, 1p31.3-p31.1, 16q24.1-24.3) have been reported for the disseminated forms of PK which include DSAP, DSP, porokeratosis palmaris et plantaris disseminata (PPPD), and immunosuppression-induced porokeratosis (ISIP) (Schamroth et al., 1997; Luan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Schamroth et al., 1997; Luan et al., 2011).

claim: The disseminated forms of PK include DSAP, DSP, porokeratosis palmaris et plantaris disseminata (PPPD), and immunosuppression-induced porokeratosis (ISIP).
source: At least five linkage loci (i.e., 12q23.2-24.1, 15q25.1-26.1, 18p11.3, 1p31.3-p31.1, 16q24.1-24.3) have been reported for the disseminated forms of PK which include DSAP, DSP, porokeratosis palmaris et plantaris disseminata (PPPD), and immunosuppression-induced porokeratosis (ISIP) (Schamroth et al., 1997; Luan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a definitional statement about PK variants, drawing from established medical knowledge and citations.

claim: Only one causal gene, the mevalonate kinase gene (MVK) at 12q24, has been identified in DSAP and porokeratosis of Mibille (PM).
source: However, only one causal gene, the mevalonate kinase gene (MVK) at 12q24, has been identified in DSAP and porokeratosis of Mibille (PM) (Zhang et al., 2012; Li and Zhang, 2014; Zeng et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Zhang et al., 2012; Li and Zhang, 2014; Zeng et al., 2014).

claim: A linkage locus for DSAP was previously identified on chromosome 16q24.1-24.3 in a four-generation Chinese DSAP family.
source: We previously identified a linkage locus for DSAP on chromosome 16q24.1-24.3 in a four-generation Chinese DSAP family (Luan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Luan et al., 2011).

claim: A c.746T>C (p.Phe249Ser) mutation in MVD was identified in a DSAP family.
source: We performed Sanger sequencing of all MVD exons and identified a c.746T>C (p.Phe249Ser) mutation in MVD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Sanger sequencing performed in the study.

claim: The c.746T>C mutation in MVD displayed 100% co-segregation with the PK phenotype in the studied family.
source: The c.746T>C mutation displayed 100% co-segregation with the PK phenotype in this family (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1, demonstrating co-segregation analysis.

claim: Both MVD and MVK are involved in isoprenoid biosynthesis via the mevalonate pathway.
source: Since both MVD and MVK are involved in isoprenoid biosynthesis via the mevalonate pathway (Thurnher et al., 2013), we hypothesized that mutations in other members of the mevalonate pathway exist in PK and screened for mutations in 12 genes in the mevalonate pathway including MVD and MVK in 134 PK patients (61 familial and 73 sporadic).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thurnher et al., 2013.

claim: Mutations in 12 genes in the mevalonate pathway were screened in 134 PK patients (61 familial and 73 sporadic).
source: Since both MVD and MVK are involved in isoprenoid biosynthesis via the mevalonate pathway (Thurnher et al., 2013), we hypothesized that mutations in other members of the mevalonate pathway exist in PK and screened for mutations in 12 genes in the mevalonate pathway including MVD and MVK in 134 PK patients (61 familial and 73 sporadic).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: The 12 genes screened are: acetyl-CoA acetyltransferase (ACAT) 1 and 2, 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA synthase (HMGCS) 1 and 2, 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA reductase (HMGCR), MVK, phosphomevalonate kinase (PMVK), MVD, isopentenyl-diphosphate delta isomerase (IDI) 1 and 2, farnesyl diphosphate synthase (FDPS), and geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthase 1 (GGPS1).
source: The 12 genes are: acetyl-CoA acetyltransferase (ACAT) 1 and 2, 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA synthase (HMGCS) 1 and 2, 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA reductase (HMGCR), MVK, phosphomevalonate kinase (PMVK), MVD, isopentenyl-diphosphate delta isomerase (IDI) 1 and 2, farnesyl diphosphate synthase (FDPS), and geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthase 1 (GGPS1) (Kanehisa et al., 2012) (Figure 2).
evidence: This lists the genes screened in the study, with reference to the KEGG database (Kanehisa et al., 2012) and Figure 2.

claim: 60 out of 61 SNVs called from NGS data were demonstrated to be true SNVs after Sanger sequencing validation.
source: After Sanger sequencing validation, 60 out of 61 SNVs called from NGS data were demonstrated to be true SNVs, which were predicted to impact protein function.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental validation data comparing NGS and Sanger sequencing results.

claim: 12 non-pathogenic SNVs were excluded from subsequent analysis.
source: Of these, 12 non-pathogenic SNVs were excluded from subsequent analysis (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the data filtering process in the study.

claim: 48 mutation sites were identified in MVK, PMVK, MVD, and FDPS.
source: In total, 48 mutation sites were identified in MVK, PMVK, MVD, and FDPS (Figure 3, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and associated source data.

claim: Three deletion mutations were identified by the CNVplex assay in samples with no confirmed point mutation in MVK, PMVK, MVD, and FDPS genes.
source: For 27 samples with no confirmed point mutation in MVK, PMVK, MVD, and FDPS genes, large deletion or duplication mutations were interrogated by analyzing the copy number of promoters and all exons in these genes. As a result, three deletion mutations were identified by the CNVplex assay.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the CNVplex assay.

claim: Three deletions were identified in four (F-26, F-40, S-69 and S-21), one (S-56) and one (F-6) cases, respectively.
source: These three deletions were identified in four (F-26, F-40, S-69 and S-21), one (S-56) and one (F-6) cases, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the CNVplex assay.

claim: In 20 pedigrees with more than two blood samples collected, all patients carried the same mutation with the proband.
source: In 20 pedigrees with more than two blood samples collected, all patients carried the same mutation with the proband.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Sanger sequencing validation in family members.

claim: No mutation was detected in any of the healthy family members.
source: On the other hand, no mutation was detected in any of the healthy family members.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Sanger sequencing validation in family members.

claim: Except for one common MVD mutation of c.746T>C, all deleterious candidate SNVs and large deletions were undetected in healthy family members and 270 unrelated ethnically matched controls.
source: Except for one common MVD mutation of c.746T>C, all deleterious candidate SNVs and large deletions were undetected in healthy family members and 270 unrelated ethnically matched controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from control sample screening.

claim: 13 mutations in MVD, six mutations in PMVK, four mutations in FDPS, and 28 mutations in MVK were identified in 113 of the 134 PK patients.
source: In total, we identified 13 mutations in MVD, six mutations in PMVK, four mutations in FDPS, and 28 mutations in MVK in 113 of the 134 PK patients (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutation screening.

claim: 21 of the 28 MVK mutations are novel.
source: Notably, 21 of the 28 MVK mutations are novel (Li and Zhang, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with previously reported mutations (Li and Zhang, 2014).

claim: The mutations include 30 missense (58%), two start codon (4%), five nonsense (10%), seven indels (14%), four splicing defects (8%), and three large deletions (6%).
source: These mutations include 30 missense (58%), two start codon (4%), five nonsense (10%), seven indels (14%), four splicing defects (8%), and three large deletions (6%), and predictably affect functions of the respective enzymes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutation screening and classification.

claim: The two MVD mutations (c.746T>C and c.875A>G) were identified in 50 unrelated patients, accounting for 81% of all patients with MVD mutations.
source: The two MVD mutations (c.746T>C and c.875A>G) were identified in 50 unrelated patients, accounting for 81% of all patients with MVD mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutation screening.

claim: Among the 60 familial patients in whom at least one mutation was found, 30 had MVD mutations, three had PMVK mutations, two had FDPS mutations, 24 had MVK mutations, and one had both MVK and MVD mutations.
source: Among the 60 familial patients in whom at least one mutation was found, 30 had MVD mutations, three had PMVK mutations, two had FDPS mutations, 24 had MVK mutations, and one had both MVK and MVD mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutation screening.

claim: Among the 53 sporadic patients in whom at least one mutation was found, 31 had MVD mutations, six had PMVK mutations, two had FDPS mutations, and 14 had MVK mutations.
source: Among the 53 sporadic patients in whom at least one mutation was found, 31 had MVD mutations, six had PMVK mutations, two had FDPS mutations, and 14 had MVK mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutation screening.

claim: No mutation was found in the remaining 21 PK patients.
source: No mutation was found in the remaining 21 PK patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutation screening.

claim: No mutation in the SLC17A9 gene was found in the 21 PK patients studied.
source: However, no mutation in the SLC17A9 gene was found in the 21 PK patients studied.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Sanger sequencing of SLC17A9.

claim: Mutations in the SLC17A9 gene were recently reported to be another genetic cause for DSAP.
source: Mutations in the SLC17A9 gene were recently reported to be another genetic cause for DSAP (Cui et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cui et al., 2014.

claim: The study included 134 index patients (92 males and 42 females) with PK.
source: To explore the genotype–phenotype correlations, we studied the clinical records of 134 index patients (92 males and 42 females) with PK.
evidence: This describes the study population.

claim: In all patients, the clinical diagnosis was supported by histopathological examinations.
source: In all patients, the clinical diagnosis was supported by histopathological examinations.
evidence: This describes the diagnostic criteria used in the study.

claim: The onset of the disease ranged from birth to 78 years (mean age 31 years).
source: The onset of the disease ranged from birth to 78 years (mean age 31 years).
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data from the study population.

claim: No malignant degeneration was found in the lesions of these patients.
source: However, no malignant degeneration was found in the lesions of these patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data from the study population.

claim: Although all affected members in the same family carried the same mutation, each affected member showed different clinical manifestations and severity.
source: Although all affected members in the same family carried the same mutation, each affected member showed different clinical manifestations and severity.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical and genetic data from the study.

claim: Giant plaque-type porokeratosis ptychotropica (PPt) with lesion diameters at least 5 cm appeared to be a unique phenotype associated with MVK mutations.
source: First, giant plaque-type porokeratosis ptychotropica (PPt) with lesion diameters at least 5 cm appeared to be a unique phenotype associated with MVK mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data showing genotype-phenotype correlations.

claim: Giant plaque-type PPt was observed in 50% (19/38) of index patients with MVK mutations, but not in any patients with MVD, PMVK, or FDPS mutations.
source: This feature was observed in 50% (19/38) of index patients with MVK mutations, but not in any patients with MVD, PMVK, or FDPS mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data showing genotype-phenotype correlations.

claim: Patients with MVK mutations generally showed the widest range of phenotypes in terms of both the number and size of lesions.
source: In addition, patients with MVK mutations generally showed the widest range of phenotypes in terms of both the number and size of lesions.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data showing genotype-phenotype correlations.

claim: Localized genital PK and porokeratoma appeared to be unique phenotypes associated with PMVK mutations.
source: Second, localized genital PK (Chen et al., 2006) and porokeratoma (Walsh et al., 2007) appeared to be unique phenotypes associated with PMVK mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data showing genotype-phenotype correlations, with references to prior descriptions of these phenotypes (Chen et al., 2006; Walsh et al., 2007).

claim: In PK patients with MVD mutations, the age of onset spanned from 5 to 70 years, and the diameter of the lesions was generally less than 2 cm.
source: Third, in PK patients with MVD mutations, the age of onset spanned from 5 to 70 years, and the diameter of the lesions was generally less than 2 cm.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data showing genotype-phenotype correlations.

claim: Five females and one male with MVD mutations manifested mild solar facial PK, which was not found in any patients with mutations in other genes.
source: Five females and one male with MVD mutations manifested mild solar facial PK (Sharquie and Al-Baghdady, 2003), which was not found in any patients with mutations in other genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data showing genotype-phenotype correlations, with reference to prior description of solar facial PK (Sharquie and Al-Baghdady, 2003).

claim: In patients with FDPS mutations, the number of lesions was generally more than 500 and the diameter of the lesions was less than 1 cm.
source: Fourth, in patients with FDPS mutations, the number of lesions was generally more than 500 and the diameter of the lesions was less than 1 cm.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data showing genotype-phenotype correlations.

claim: The lesions harboring mutations in MVD and FDPS genes tended to be more homogeneous and superficial than those carrying mutations in MVK and PMVK genes.
source: As a whole, the lesions harboring mutations in MVD and FDPS genes tended to be more homogeneous and superficial than those carrying mutations in MVK and PMVK genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data showing genotype-phenotype correlations.

claim: The phenotypes of MVD and FDPS mutations on the natal cleft were mild and unobvious.
source: The phenotypes of MVD and FDPS mutations on the natal cleft were mild and unobvious.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data showing genotype-phenotype correlations.

claim: Some patients harboring MVK and PMVK mutations firstly presented with untypical lesions of genitogluteal porokeratosis (GGP).
source: However, some patients harboring MVK and PMVK mutations firstly presented with untypical lesions of genitogluteal porokeratosis (GGP).
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data showing genotype-phenotype correlations.

claim: The expression of the wild allele in 10 out of 13 LTs was significantly reduced at the 1% significance level.
source: The expression of the wild allele in 10 out of 13 LTs was significantly reduced at the 1% significance level (Figures 5–7, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from AEI assays shown in Figures 5-7 and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The expression of the mutant allele was significantly reduced in almost all NNS (except one from F-42) carrying a mutation resulting in nonsense, frameshift, or splicing defect.
source: In contrast, the expression of the mutant allele was significantly reduced in almost all NNS (except one from F-42) carrying a mutation resulting in nonsense, frameshift, or splicing defect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from AEI assays.

claim: For LT from F-31, the mutant to wild allelic ratio in genomic DNA was >3 compared with the ratio of about 1 in the corresponding NNS genomic DNA.
source: As for LT from F-31, the mutant to wild allelic ratio in genomic DNA was >3 compared with the ratio of about 1 in the corresponding NNS genomic DNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from AEI assays.

claim: Gene conversion of the wild to the mutant allele might have occurred in the LT from F-31.
source: However, no deletion or duplication of all MVK exons was detected in F-31, which might indicate that gene conversion of the wild to the mutant allele occurred in the LT (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed allelic ratio and absence of copy number changes.

claim: Gene conversion might also occur in the thigh LT of F-43.
source: Gene conversion might also occur in the thigh LT of F-43 (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: No copy number change or CpG island methylation was detected at the corresponding mutated genes in all LTs.
source: No copy number change or CpG island methylation was detected at the corresponding mutated genes in all LTs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CNVplex assay and bisulfite sequencing.

claim: A mutation of c.1003G>A (p.Gly335Ser) on the wild allele (T) of MVK: c.1093T>A was identified in the cDNA of the LT without AEI but not the cDNA of NNS collected from the left forearm of F-38.
source: A mutation of c.1003G>A (p.Gly335Ser) on the wild allele (T) of MVK: c.1093T>A was identified in the cDNA of the LT without AEI but not the cDNA of NNS collected from the left forearm of F-38 (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cDNA sequencing shown in Figure 6.

claim: The mutation of c.1003G>A was not identified in the genomic DNA of the LT from F-38, which indicated that G-to-A RNA editing occurred on the wild allele of MVK: c.1093T>A.
source: Surprisingly, this mutation of c.1003G>A was not identified in the genomic DNA of this LT either, which indicated that G-to-A RNA editing occurred on the wild allele of MVK: c.1093T>A.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of the mutation in cDNA but not genomic DNA.

claim: No mutation was observed in cDNA samples from other tissues.
source: No mutation was observed in cDNA samples from other tissues.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cDNA sequencing.

claim: Mutations were identified in four genes (MVK, PMVK, MVD, and FDPS) underlying PK by massively parallel sequencing and copy number variation analysis in 134 index patients with PK.
source: In this present study we were able to identify mutations in four genes (MVK, PMVK, MVD, and FDPS) underlying PK by massively parallel sequencing and copy number variation analysis in 134 index patients with PK.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: In the 12 PK families where the affected members span three to six generations, mutations were found only in MVK or MVD but not in PMVK or FDPS.
source: In the 12 PK families where the affected members span three to six generations, we found mutations only in MVK or MVD but not in PMVK or FDPS (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Correlation of genotypes and several clinical manifestations in the PK patients was observed, which might be helpful to simplify the classification of PK under the guidance of genetic testing.
source: We also observed the correlation of genotypes and several clinical manifestations in the PK patients (Table 1), which might be helpful to simplify the classification of PK under the guidance of genetic testing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed genotype-phenotype correlations shown in Table 1.

claim: Two patients were identified to carry two mutations: c.302C>G (p.Pro101Arg) and c.683G>A (p.Arg228Gln) in MVD for S-62, and c.746T>C (p.Phe249Ser) in MVD and c.235G>A (p.Asp79Asn) in MVK for F-28.
source: Interestingly, two patients were identified to carry two mutations: c.302C>G (p.Pro101Arg) and c.683G>A (p.Arg228Gln) in MVD for S-62, and c.746T>C (p.Phe249Ser) in MVD and c.235G>A (p.Asp79Asn) in MVK for F-28.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutation screening.

claim: The two mutations in MVD for S-62 were located in the trans position, for his daughter carried only one of them.
source: The two mutations in MVD for S-62 were located in the trans position, for his daughter carried only one of them (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: S-62 had late-onset PK at the age of 50 and his 30-year-old daughter had no lesions to date.
source: S-62 had late-onset PK at the age of 50 and his 30-year-old daughter had no lesions to date.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data from the study.

claim: Index patients F-28 and S-62 did not present with more severe phenotypes or earlier age of onset or any other unique clinical features.
source: According to our observation, index patients F-28 and S-62 did not present with more severe phenotypes or earlier age of onset or any other unique clinical features.
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical data from the study.

claim: 21 patients without detected pathogenic mutations included five cases with linear PK (LP), six cases with solitary plaque-type PK, and 10 cases with disseminated PK (only one had family history).
source: In this study we did not detect pathogenic mutation in 21 patients: five cases with linear PK (LP), six cases with solitary plaque-type PK, and 10 cases with disseminated PK (only one had family history).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mutation screening.

claim: G-to-A RNA editing in PK was first reported in this study.
source: G-to-A RNA editing in PK was first reported in our study.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cDNA sequencing showing RNA editing.

claim: The RNA editing seemed to occur selectively on the one copy of MVK and this selective editing pattern seemed to be capable of being transmitted during mitosis.
source: Interestingly, the RNA editing seemed to occur selectively on the one copy of MVK and this selective editing pattern seemed to be capable of being transmitted during mitosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed selective RNA editing pattern.

claim: The expression of wild allele was significantly reduced to various extents in most LTs (>77%).
source: Using AEI assays, we observed that the expression of wild allele was significantly reduced to various extents in most LTs (>77%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from AEI assays.

claim: The variation in the expression reduction level might be due to the LT containing various amounts of normal-appearing keratinocytes and other different types of cells.
source: The variation in the expression reduction level might be due to the LT containing various amounts of normal-appearing keratinocytes and other different types of cells.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed variation in expression reduction.

claim: Somatic loss of function of the wild allele in the epidermal stem cells might play a key role in the formation of lesions.
source: Somatic loss of function of the wild allele in the epidermal stem cells might play a key role in the formation of lesions, and it might occur spontaneously and be induced by environmental factors such as ultraviolet light.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism of lesion formation.

claim: Somatic loss of function of the wild allele might occur spontaneously and be induced by environmental factors such as ultraviolet light.
source: Somatic loss of function of the wild allele in the epidermal stem cells might play a key role in the formation of lesions, and it might occur spontaneously and be induced by environmental factors such as ultraviolet light.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism of somatic loss of function.

claim: The somatic loss of function of the wild allele in LTs of PK could be mainly caused by suppression of the wild allele through gene conversion in a minor proportion of cases or an unknown DNA methylation-independent epigenetic mechanism in most cases.
source: There was only one RNA editing identified in the LT, therefore the somatic loss of function of the wild allele in LTs of PK could be mainly caused by suppression of the wild allele through gene conversion in a minor proportion of cases or an unknown DNA methylation-independent epigenetic mechanism in most cases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed data and the rarity of RNA editing.

claim: Allelic imbalance of histone methylation modification unlinked to DNA methylation, whose pattern is able to be transmitted during cell mitosis, could be the DNA methylation-independent epigenetic mechanism.
source: Allelic imbalance of histone methylation modification unlinked to DNA methylation, whose pattern is able to be transmitted during cell mitosis, could be the DNA methylation-independent epigenetic mechanism (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the epigenetic mechanism, with reference to Xu et al., 2011.

claim: Reduced expression or somatic mutation of the wild allele was not found in only two LTs.
source: We did not find reduced expression or somatic mutation of the wild allele in only two LTs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from AEI assays and mutation screening.

claim: The LT might contain many normal cells affecting the sensitivity of AEI and mutation detection.
source: The reason for this could be that the LT might contain many normal cells affecting the sensitivity of AEI and mutation detection.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of detected changes in some LTs.

claim: Gene conversion of the wild allele to the mutant allele was first identified in this study as a starter button of PK.
source: As a starter button of PK, gene conversion of the wild allele to the mutant allele was first identified in this study.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing gene conversion in lesional tissues.

claim: This observation is generally consistent with the phenomenon known as 'revertant mosaicism', in which the mutant allele is corrected in some stem cells.
source: This observation is generally consistent with the phenomenon known as 'revertant mosaicism', in which the mutant allele is corrected in some stem cells.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observed gene conversion to the known phenomenon of revertant mosaicism.

claim: Revertant mosaicism is mainly identified in blood diseases such as Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome and Fanconi's anemia, and skin diseases such as ichthyosis and epidermolysis bullosa.
source: Revertant mosaicism is mainly identified in blood diseases such as Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome and Fanconi's anemia, and skin diseases such as ichthyosis and epidermolysis bullosa (May, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to May, 2011.

claim: Gene conversion could be a natural 'rescue angel' in some recessive diseases or a 'damaging devil' in some dominant diseases.
source: Therefore, gene conversion could be a natural 'rescue angel' in some recessive diseases or a 'damaging devil' in some dominant diseases, which could mostly affect tissues with extensive ability to self-renew for life.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the implications of gene conversion.

claim: Mendelian diseases can be caused by multiple genes involved in the same metabolic or signal transduction pathway, or producing proteins on interaction.
source: Our findings support the notion that Mendelian diseases can be caused by multiple genes involved in the same metabolic or signal transduction pathway, or producing proteins on interaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings that multiple genes in the mevalonate pathway cause PK.

claim: The mevalonate pathway of isoprenoid biosynthesis provides precursors of isoprenoids, which are ubiquitous in living species and diverse in biological function.
source: The mevalonate pathway of isoprenoid biosynthesis provides precursors of isoprenoids, which are ubiquitous in living species and diverse in biological function (Smit and Mushegian, 2000) and serve as precursors of cholesterol, heme A, ubiquinones, dolichol, and isoprenylated proteins (e.g., RAS and Lamin B) (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Smit and Mushegian, 2000, and illustrated in Figure 2.
